title: The timeline of Verstappen and Russell’s long rivalry
excerpt:
The Las Vegas Grand Prix proved to be an unforgettable, action-packed race – but there was also drama unfolding off the track, with an incident between Max Verstappen and George Russell in third practice leading to tensions once again flaring between the pair. F1.com charts the story of the rivalry so far, which was first ignited more than three years ago…

April 2023 – Tensions sparked by Sprint fight

Back in 2023, Verstappen was challenged by a fast-starting Russell for P3 as the Sprint at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix got underway. The pair went wheel-to-wheel through several corners and made contact along the way, before Verstappen later reclaimed third place.

The Dutch driver was seen surveying the damage to his car in parc ferme after the event – with a sizeable hole visible on the side of the Red Bull – and then shared a frosty exchange with Russell in front of the cameras.

Speaking to the media afterwards, Verstappen said that the situation was “not clarified” after their discussion, adding: “I just don’t understand why you need to take so much risk on Lap 1. Understeering into my sidepod, created a hole…

“We all have cold tyres, it’s all easy to lock up, but in his beautiful way of explaining, ‘Oh mate, locked up, look at the onboard’, it doesn’t make sense. It’s fine, we still got into P3, got some good points, but it is what it is.”

Russell said that he was taken aback when Verstappen confronted him post-Sprint, commenting: “I was quite surprised, I thought he was coming over to say ‘good battle’, to be honest.

“I’m here to fight, I’m here to win. I’m not just going to wave him by because he’s Max Verstappen in a Red Bull. [There’s] nothing really more to say. I thought the move was on and that’s about it, really.”

November 2024 – Verstappen hit with penalty after Russell incident

Over one year on, trouble brewed again at the penultimate round of the 2024 season in Qatar.

Verstappen and Russell were summoned to the stewards on Saturday night following an incident between them in Qualifying, with Verstappen being investigated for driving unnecessarily slowly on a cooldown lap which Russell felt he had been impeded by.

Following the stewards’ hearing, it was confirmed that Verstappen – who had originally claimed pole position ahead of Russell – had been handed a one-place grid penalty.

In a document released afterwards, the stewards noted that Russell had stated that "if a car was going slow in a high-speed corner, it should not be on the racing line", but they concluded that the case was "a complicated one" and did not warrant the usual three-place grid penalty as neither driver was on a push lap.

All the key moments from the Las Vegas Grand Prix

December 2024 – War of words escalates as Verstappen ‘loses respect’ for Russell

That grid drop did not deter Verstappen, who went on to win the race while Russell crossed the line in fourth. In the post-race press conference, the Red Bull driver admitted that he “couldn’t believe” that he was given the penalty.

He then shared his thoughts on the role that Russell had played in the process and stated that he had “lost all respect” for the Mercedes racer.

“I was quite surprised when sitting there in the stewards’ room [about] what was all going on,” said Verstappen.

“Honestly, [it was] very disappointing because I think we're all here, we respect each other a lot and of course, I've been in that meeting room many times in my life, in my career, with people that I’ve raced and I've never seen someone trying to screw someone over that hard. And that for me… I lost all respect.”

December 2024 – Russell fires back at Verstappen for ‘crossing a line’

A few days later, the paddock assembled in Abu Dhabi for the season finale – where Russell was quizzed for the first time on Verstappen’s remarks. The Briton spoke at length about the topic, firstly stating that what happened on the track was “not personal” to him.

“It’s part of racing, but the words he said [are] totally unnecessary,” said Russell. “He’s crossed a line and I’m not going to accept it, so somebody has to stand up to someone who thinks he’s above the law.”

On the incident, he added: “It wasn’t crazy dangerous, and was the penalty harsh? Maybe it was a little bit harsh, but these are the rules. We all have the rules and we all have to follow it.”

Russell went on to comment: “I’ve known Max for 12 years, I’ve respected him all of this time, but now I’ve lost respect for him because we’re all fighting on track and it’s never personal. Now he’s made it personal, and someone needs to stand up to a bully like this. So far, people let him get away with murder.”

The British driver also voiced his belief that Verstappen “lashes out with unnecessary anger and borderline violence” when things are not going his way, and stated that he wished the Dutchman would “be a better role model”.

June 2025 – Dramatic collision reignites tensions

A few months on, F1 went racing in Barcelona for Round 9 of the 2025 championship. When the race was restarted in the latter stages following a Safety Car phase, Verstappen found himself under pressure from Russell in a battle for fourth place.

There was contact between the pair and Verstappen was forced to go down the escape road, with Red Bull telling their driver to hand the position back. Another collision then occurred, leading Russell to comment over the radio: “He just crashed into me.”

Verstappen was subsequently handed a 10-second time penalty for the incident, dropping him down to a final result of P10 while Russell held onto P4.

Giving his perspective on the clash afterwards, Russell said: “I don’t really know why or what the thinking was behind it. In the end, I’m glad that I continued with little damage and ultimately it punished him a lot more than me.

“That’s how Max goes racing. As I said, he was in P4, I was in P5 – I ended up P4, he ended up P10, so from my side I’m glad that I managed to finish the race. Not really sure what he was thinking because he cost himself and his team a lot of points, so no conversation [is] really required.”

Verstappen kept his take on the collision brief, commenting: “I don’t need to say anything about it because it doesn’t matter anyway.”

June 2025 – Russell surprised by Verstappen’s later comments

One day on from the collision, Verstappen wrote in a social media post that the move he made on Russell “was not right and shouldn’t have happened”, adding that “our tyre choice at the end and some moves after the [Safety Car] restart fuelled my frustration”.

“I always give everything out there for the team and emotions can run high,” the World Champion continued. “You win some together, you lose some together.”

Ahead of the next race on the calendar in Canada, Russell argued that Verstappen was "just trying to get his elbows out and show who's boss" rather than committing a deliberate or premeditated act, before insisting that there were no issues between them.

“Obviously it would have been a different feeling had it taken me out of the race but ultimately I benefitted from it and he was penalised,” Russell explained.

“I was a bit surprised to see he had taken responsibility, so fine. But I haven't spoken to him about it. We actually bumped into each other at the airport the other day but I actually completely forgot we crashed into each other a few days prior. No issues.”

Verstappen 'from a different planet' – Mekies

June 2025 – Wolff reacts as Verstappen to Mercedes speculation emerges

After a mixed start to the season for Red Bull, rumours began to emerge during the summer linking Verstappen with a move to Mercedes – given that the Silver Arrows had yet to confirm their 2026 line-up.

Russell admitted that it was “only normal that conversations with the likes of Verstappen are ongoing” but insisted that he continued to feel positive about his own future at the squad, telling Sky Sports F1: “From my side, if I'm performing as I'm doing, what have I got to be concerned about? There are two seats in every Formula 1 team.”

Reflecting on the speculation, Mercedes Team Principal Toto Wolff acknowledged that there were “some conversations you just simply need to have” whilst reiterating that his intention was to continue with Russell and Kimi Antonelli.

Wolff was also quizzed on whether Verstappen and Russell could ever race together, given the previous tensions between the two.

“I can imagine every line-up,” he responded. “I had [Nico] Rosberg and [Lewis] Hamilton fighting for a World Championship, so everything else afterwards is easy. There's pros and cons of having two drivers fighting each other hard. We've seen examples where that functioned and other examples where it didn't.”

July 2025 – Verstappen confirms future with Red Bull

Ahead of F1’s traditional summer break, Verstappen was asked whether his and Wolff's yachts might be located near to each other during the holidays – amid the continued speculation about Mercedes talks – but confirmed that he would be staying with Red Bull in 2026.

“I'm discussing with the team already the plans, the things that we want to change next year so that means I'm also staying with the team for next year,” he answered. “And if my boat is next to Toto's then the boat is next to Toto's.

"You can have a personal relationship with someone even if you don't have a working relationship with someone."

He also added to the media: “I think it's time to basically stop all the rumours, and for me it's always been quite clear that I was staying anyway."

Russell and Antonelli, meanwhile, were confirmed as Mercedes’ 2026 line-up a few months later in October – meaning that the potentially fascinating scenario of Russell and Verstappen becoming team mates would not be on the cards in the near future.

November 2026 – Russell criticises Verstappen over practice incident

Fast-forward to the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix, and Russell and Verstappen were summoned to the stewards once again following an incident between them in the third and final practice session on Friday.

Verstappen braked earlier than expected ahead of Russell and changed direction under braking before the pair made contact as they went wheel-to-wheel into Turn 14, with Verstappen subsequently receiving a warning for driving erratically.

Russell was critical of the Red Bull driver when speaking to Sky Italia after Qualifying – ahead of the pair lining up alongside each other on the front row for Saturday’s race, which each promoted one position following a penalty for the pace-setting Antonelli.

“I think the warning was fine,” Russell commented. “There's nothing in the rules to say that you cannot overtake someone who is starting their lap but when you do this, you are screwing this person over.

“He does this week in, week out, with many drivers. Everybody accepts it and I am not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they are bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."

November 2026 – Verstappen claims Russell is ‘so far below my level’

On the night of the race in Las Vegas, Verstappen and Russell spent much of a breathless Grand Prix exchanging places at the front of the pack, with Russell making a number of overtakes only for the Dutchman to retake P1 moments later.

Antonelli had also joined the battle by the latter stages, moving up into second ahead of Russell. The latter then tried to get back in front of his team mate but the move backfired, the Briton having locked up before hitting the barriers.

While he was able to continue, this dropped him down to P9 – and it was a sequence of events that did not go unnoticed by race winner Verstappen, who gave his reaction to what happened as well as addressing Russell’s comments from one day earlier during the post-race press conference.

“The thing is, he speaks a lot next to the track, and honestly for me it doesn’t really bother me because he’s so far below my level that it doesn’t really make any sense for me anyway to try and challenge that, so it doesn’t bother me,” said Verstappen.

“And today, karma is a b****. It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and I saw what was happening, so I was like, ‘Fantastic – my day is only getting better’. Of course when I then crossed the line in first, my day was complete.”

November 2026 – Russell defends his move

Russell later defended his attempted overtake in a social media post shared a few hours after the Grand Prix.

“I wanted that win today,” the Mercedes driver explained. “It was a bizarre race and I went for a high risk move and paid the price.

“Of course I’m disappointed with the outcome, however, I have no regrets. I fought and knew if I wanted the win, I needed to be in the top two positions into the final laps.”

With only a few days remaining until the action resumes again at the Qatar Grand Prix, the ongoing dispute is likely to be a hot topic during Thursday’s media day…

title: Sainz hails ‘amazing’ Las Vegas GP after ‘incredible’ P8
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz enjoyed an "amazing" drive in Las Vegas as the Spaniard managed to bring his Williams home in eighth place, scoring for the first time since Baku.

Having qualified 14th, Sainz started down in P20 after a 10-place grid drop for taking a new turbocharger. His quest to make up places off the line was made slightly easier by two cars starting ahead not taking to the grid – his team mate being one of them, as Alex Albon was unable to start the race due to overheating brakes.

But Sainz still had a lot of work to do from the rear of the field, and he was proud of what he achieved throughout the 50-lap Grand Prix.

“Just amazing, honestly didn’t expect it yesterday when starting almost last, to get P8 in a year when we have struggling so much," he said. "I said this weekend was maybe our only opportunity to score points in the second half of the year, and the opportunity presented itself.

“I did an amazing start, incredible Lap 1 and then a great race. I think 50 qualifying laps to stay around cars that were obviously quicker than us, being strategic with deployment, being strategic with my overtaking and my slipstreaming.

“I managed to stay in the fight and managed to score four points for the team that I am sure is going to motivate everyone.”

Sainz climbed up the order in the opening stint before benefitting from a pit stop behind the Safety Car, which was called following a clash between Sergio Perez and Rafael Camara.

With many teams having to double stack their drivers Sainz, as the only Williams on the track, was able to get in for fresh rubber and get back out swiftly, climbing into the top 10 as a result.

From there he did not panic as some faster cars recovered back past the Williams, instead using his deployment wisely in a drive reminiscent of his win for Ferrari in Singapore in 2023, where he deliberately dropped back to give Lando Norris behind DRS, to keep other faster cars at bay.

“I think the team knows we shouldn’t get any points in the rest of the year, that’s why this was our only and last chance, given the relative competitiveness in other tracks,” Sainz said.

“I think I am just proud the team nailed a very good weekend together with me, we both did an incredible team effort to – the only chance that we had this year to get points, we managed to take it, which continues a bit the trend from last year, whenever we had podium opportunities, we took them.

“This year, whenever we have had point opportunities, we have taken them and executed very good weekends.”

But while there was joy on one side of the garage, there was despair on the other. Albon had been due to start 14th in Las Vegas, six places higher than his team mate, but his car was wheeled off the grid with overheating brakes, an unusual issue in the cool Vegas conditions.

Sadly, the team could not rectify the issue before the race began, leaving Albon with his second DNS of the season.

“You need a lot of blanking to keep the stuff that’s cold warm, we don’t really understand it at the moment, we’ll have a look,” he said afterwards. “[It’s] frustrating, that’s pretty much the year so far. We’ll see what we can do in the next few races.”

title: Perez and Camara react to Las Vegas GP clash
excerpt:
Sergio Perez and Rafael Camara have each given their take on the moment they collided during the Las Vegas Grand Prix, an incident that saw Perez receive a grid penalty for next weekend’s race in Qatar.

The Cadillac driver had been attempting to overtake Camara on the approach to Turn 14 – as the race neared its halfway point – but made contact with the rear left tyre on the Haas, sending both cars into the barriers.

Camara was able to rejoin and finish the race while Perez found himself out of the running, with the Safety Car subsequently deployed. The stewards later found Perez at fault when the incident was investigated and handed him a five-place grid drop for the next event he participates in, that being the upcoming Qatar Grand Prix.

Reflecting on the clash after jumping out of the car, Perez explained: “I just spoke to Camara and he said that he didn't see me, because it's a bit weird – you exit Turn 12, like one second behind, which is a massive distance, and then you are halfway down the straight alongside.

“And unfortunately he didn’t see me so I was alongside him and, when I saw that he basically did the corner as if I wasn't there, and when I tried to avoid it, it was just too late.”

Despite the disappointing end to his race, the Mexican took heart from how the car had been performing prior to that.

“We were in the mix,” he added. “We stayed in racing with the Overtake Mode and we were fighting other cars, which was good. The race was going well up to that point.”

Camara, meanwhile, admitted that he needed more time to assess what had happened with Perez as he looked back on how his second F1 race had unfolded, having crossed the line in P16.

“I think at some parts it was quite fun,” the Brazilian said. “We had some overtakes and it's always nice to be battling, but in the end it was a bit more boring being alone the whole race, and then at the end I got overtook by Isack [Hadjar] and [Liam] Lawson.

“But no, I think it was positive race. I think also through the race I was always improving myself inside the car. I think the start was a bit tricky to get the tyres in temp and get a good first lap, but I think once we had everything under control, I think it was a decent race.

“Obviously there was the touch with Checo, but I still need to see what happened there exactly.”

It has since been confirmed that Camara will again race for Haas at the Qatar and Abu Dhabi Grands Prix ahead of his full-time debut in 2027, but – speaking before this was announced – the 21-year-old conceded that the experience he had gained in Sao Paulo and Las Vegas had already proven beneficial.

“Everything that happened was very positive,” he explained. “I think it's very rare to get some laps before you start your full season with an F1 car doing the races.

“Obviously we have the testing, but a race weekend is always a bit different and I think that was very useful. And yeah, now we just need to see what will happen, and whatever happens we're going to be ready.”

title: Gasly reveals issue as he felt he could challenge for Vegas win
excerpt:
Pierre Gasly was one of the stars of a thrilling Las Vegas Grand Prix as the Alpine driver battled with drivers from the top four teams for the whole race.

On more than one occasion he popped into P3, and at one stage he even thought that he might have a shot at victory.

As late as the last lap he got ahead of Kimi Antonelli to briefly hold fourth, although the Mercedes driver repassed him before the flag, and he thus had to settle for P5.

All of this was achieved despite his performance being compromised for much of the race by a need to keep a lid on his power unit temperatures. Although he missed out on a potential podium finish Gasly insisted that he wasn’t frustrated.

“I'm not going to call it that way,” he said. “I'll start with the fact that it's our best race as a team, and we're definitely going take the positives. I'll follow with the fact that it was a very fun race to be part of, and I enjoyed a lot battling at the front of the pack.

“At the start we were flying. I managed to find my way all the way up to P3. At that point, I really felt that we had the pace to maybe even challenge for the win. And the moment I got to P3, I got told on the radio that the car was overheating, and I had to turn down the power. And we turned down the power for 45 laps.”

Inevitably the impact on performance was costly, as Gasly added: “The moment I went to the most aggressive switch to cool it down, I lost a position on the way to Turn 5, I lost a position on the back straight, so I lost two positions in a lap.

“And then I just dropped back all the way, and then we were managing the temperature. I had to open the gap – I could be on the gearbox, but I had to open the gap to cool down the car.

“So yeah, I really feel we had the podium, and I kept asking to get back to the full power, but I was only allowed to do it for the last two laps.

Racing Bulls drivers reflect on no points in Las Vegas GP

“We'll review exactly what happened, because I can see you guys all wearing winter jackets, I am wearing a winter jacket, and I don't really understand why the car was overheating! Apart from that, it was an incredible effort from all the team.”

Given the temperatures, Gasly conceded that the team hadn’t anticipated the cooling issue.

“I don't think we saw it coming,” he said. “But this 45 laps thing, the most extreme, I think I was losing over a second a lap with that slowest engine mode that we were running.

"So happy to be to be fifth. But definitely the car was very fast, and there was more to take.”

He also detailed how much he thoroughly enjoyed being in the thick of the action, with places changing every lap.

“It was quite fun to see how everybody was kind of playing their game,” he said. “On my side I really enjoyed battling at the front of the pack; we battled with McLaren, battled with Ferrari, Kimi on the last lap. So it was good to be up there.

“At some point in the race I was like, this feels a bit like Tour de France. You've got to be in the peloton and save your legs! Basically, that's what we did. It was like we're saving our legs for the last sprint when we were managing the engine for the last few laps. It was fun.”

On a good evening for Alpine Franco Colapinto backed up his team mate with a solid P6 finish. It wasn’t a straightforward race for the Argentine driver, who tumbled down the order in the early laps. However, he was able to recover after switching to medium tyres.

“The first stint on the used soft was very poor, had no grip,” He noted. “When you put [on] a used tyre from Qualifying, you slide a lot, and it doesn't perform as well. When I put the new medium, the car performed much better, I had much more grip, so I was in a much better place, and much more competitive.

“So we could overtake, we would make the moves. And I think just for the team after a tough couple of rounds it's very positive to be fighting up there. And being back in the points with both cars in the top six is very, very good.”

title: Verstappen 'from a different planet' – Mekies
excerpt:
Laurent Mekies believes Max Verstappen is "from a different planet" after the Red Bull driver "outsmarted the opposition" on his way to victory in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The Dutchman started from pole and officially led 45 out of 50 laps on the streets of Las Vegas, with the remaining five split between Mercedes drivers George Russell and Kimi Antonelli.

However, the race featured 35 changes of lead with the long back straight and energy management creating pack racing and producing a slipstreaming thriller, one which Verstappen mastered.

The four-time World Champion almost immediately regained the lead every time he lost it, and even had the foresight to ask the team if there was anything he could do differently once the crucial final lap rolled around, only to be told that he was already doing an optimal job.

“I think Max clearly outsmarted the opposition today in the way he has managed to defend for 50 laps,” said Red Bull Team Principal Mekies.

“And yes, he has been overtaken a few times. I kind of think that he probably made it on purpose a few times, and he has probably explored every possible way around what's happening between the second to last and the last corner to the line.

“To the extent where, as you have seen, when he has asked us to have another look at scenarios for the final lap. And obviously the guys were thinking about that as well for quite a while.

“The conclusion when we came back to him was that he was already mastering it, and had explored all the options, so we felt he knew exactly what to do at that moment, and it proved to be that case.

“I think he's done another outstanding race, an exceptional race. I don't know if it's one he will remember more than the other ones, but I think it was breathtaking the way he resisted the pressure for that much.”

The win was Verstappen's fourth in the 2026 campaign, all of which have come across the last six Grands Prix, and having finished on the podium in the other two in the USA and Sao Paulo, the latter from the back of the grid.

Verstappen responds to Russell comments as rivalry reignites

When asked if some might consider his contributions underrated given the frequency of them, Mekies said: “Absolutely.

"I think you are spot-on there. We are coming from Brazil, and what he did in Brazil felt normal to everyone, where it was completely mind-blowing. And you come here, and he was asking us questions about the last lap at 10 laps to go.

“Look at the race today. Look at the race in Brazil. Look at the way he positions his car relative to the others. He is always at the perfect place, at the perfect moment. It’s surprising us every day.

“Every race on the pit wall, we look at each other and we say, 'What was that?' Because that's really what we do. I don't know if you want to call it underrated, because I don't think he's underrated – but he's from a different planet.”

title: Why Norris and Piastri had 'one of their best races' in Vegas
excerpt:
The Las Vegas Grand Prix saw a superb performance from McLaren as Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri finished second and third in a race that at one stage looked set to be dominated by the Red Bull and Mercedes drivers.

What made the final result even more impressive was that Piastri started from P17 with a power unit grid penalty, and in the early laps an apparently struggling Norris tumbled out of the top 10.

And yet both men found performance when it mattered and fought their way to the front of the field, with Norris even briefly figuring in the lead.

As Team Principal Andrea Stella made clear the result was due to a combination of good work by the drivers and the team that overcame some built-in compromises in the MCL40 package.

“There's three factors I would mention today,” said Stella. “One factor is the car didn't have inherently enough top speed, which has nothing to do with the power unit, because it's the same for all the HPP cars. There was simply too much aerodynamic drag.

“The second factor is that we pay the price of having the eighth gear too short, which is a problem, especially when you are following somebody. The revs go too high, and the power drops too much.

“And the third factor is that – and I want to praise here the work of the engineers, HPP and McLaren – the engineers figured out what was going on with Lando, why we were losing those positions, and what was working with Oscar, who was gaining positions.

“So they worked more than ever before this season with the drivers to optimise the power unit deployment. What to do with the buttons? What to do with the basic strategy?

“So I think good news in terms of exploitation of the power unit, but some other limitations, aerodynamic drag and the ratios were a problem today. But the good work of Oscar and Lando and the engineers kind of compensated for these limitations.”

Stella admitted that in effect the drivers had outperformed the package they had been given.

Norris reflects on 'chaotic' Las Vegas GP recovery

“In terms of drivers, let me say that I think for both Oscar and Lando this is one of their best races,” he said. “Because the ratio between the outcome, what they were able to extract in terms of result, and what the team made available in terms of potential of the car, I think is one of the best for both.

“I was very concerned about our raceability, a combination, like I said before, of the top speed and the ratios. And somehow Lando and Oscar figured out how to use even the slipstream.

“And when, for other cars it would have been okay to move away from the slipstream, and complete an overtaking, they realised, don't do it, because we are not even going to be able to overtake.

“So there was a lot to process while you were pretty much full bandwidth just keeping the car on track, and watching the mirrors and watching ahead. Therefore, I would like to praise definitely very clearly that this is one of the best races for Oscar and Lando.”

For Piastri in particular the Las Vegas race was hugely encouraging as we approach the end of what has been a difficult season for the Australian.

He’s been working closely with his engineering team to get more out of the car and power unit, and that appeared to have been paid off at the kind of low grip track that doesn’t usually play to his strengths.

“It's a collective effort,” said Stella. “Already in Brazil I was quite pleased with the improvement we saw in Oscar's pace, because in Brazil he lost time in the race just because of some traffic situations.

“Otherwise, he was actually racing for important positions, and this didn't show up in the final result. But the pace we saw that he had there, here it was much clearer that in addition to power unit utilisation and driving at low grip, I think Oscar drove with confidence and assertiveness.

“Which means that he is now kind of in tune with the car. He can start using his superpower, which is this racing ability, this focus – and that's very promising for the end of the season, and what we carry into the next one.”

title: Lewis Hamilton crowned world champion amid F1-rule controversy – On This Day
excerpt:
On this day 12 years ago, Lewis Hamilton became a two-time world champion.

12 years ago today, Lewis Hamilton won the 2014 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix at Yas Marina Circuit to clinch his second Formula 1 world championship, beating Mercedes team-mate Nico Rosberg to the title in a season finale that carried double points.

Hamilton started second on the grid behind Rosberg, who had taken pole with a lap of 1m40.480 to the Briton's 1m40.866.

But the race swung decisively in Hamilton's favour on lap 24, when Rosberg's car suffered an energy recovery system failure that caused a severe loss of power.

The malfunction also compromised the rear braking performance on Rosberg's Mercedes, sending him tumbling from second place all the way down to 14th at the finish.

Hamilton controlled the race from there, crossing the line to take his 11th win of the campaign. Felipe Massa finished second for Williams, with team-mate Valtteri Bottas completing the podium in third.

Daniel Ricciardo took fourth for Red Bull and set the fastest lap, while Jenson Button rounded out the top five for McLaren.

Driver

Lewis Hamilton

British

44

The controversial double points system

Because 2014's finale carried double points, a rule the FIA and F1's Strategy Group had introduced to keep the title fight alive until the last round, Hamilton's win was worth 50 points rather than the usual 25.

It secured the championship with his tally of 384 points finishing well clear of Rosberg's 317, with Ricciardo third on 238.

The format had been deeply unpopular before a wheel had even turned. Sebastian Vettel had condemned the idea as absurd when it was first announced, arguing it devalued a season's work, as reported by Sport Bild.

Toto Wolff had likewise admitted to Sky Sports F1 that he feared an artificial swing could overshadow the outcome of the title.

As it happened, Hamilton topped the standings with or without the weighting, meaning the double points made no difference to the destination of the trophy. That did nothing to quiet the backlash.

Teams had agreed to the system through the Strategy Group and F1 Commission in late 2013, but remorse set in quickly, and the FIA World Motor Sport Council scrapped the rule entirely ahead of the following season, restoring F1 to a single points system that has remained ever since.

title: Max Verstappen stuns as George Russell stumbles - Las Vegas GP Winners and Losers
excerpt:
Find out who has made RacingNews365's list of winners and losers from the Las Vegas Grand Prix!

The Las Vegas Grand Prix was a busy race that saw a record-breaking number of overtakes throughout the field.

Max Verstappen secured another race victory as he fended off a number of rival drivers to secure the top spot.

The four-time champion is an easy pick as a 'winner' from the race weekend - but who else can walk away from the race weekend with smiles on their faces?

And who faced a torrid weekend, leaving them to be judged as 'losers' from the event? Find out below!

Winners

Max Verstappen

Verstappen delivered from pole to flag in Las Vegas, but the win was anything but routine. The Red Bull driver had to repeatedly fend off various rivals, with the lead changing hands several times as the pair traded slipstream moves down the Strip's long straights.

The Dutchman's task was eased when Russell crashed into the barriers in the closing stages and Kimi Antonelli suffered an energy issue, but Verstappen had already shown the pace to match the Mercedes challenge lap after lap.

It capped a weekend that continued Red Bull's blistering finish to the 2026 campaign.

Alpine

Alpine's low-downforce approach paid off handsomely on the Strip. The French outfit ran an aggressive, straight-line-focused set-up suited to the circuit's high-speed sections, and found an ideal tyre-warm-up window in the cool Las Vegas conditions.

Pierre Gasly brought that pace home in fifth, while Franco Colapinto backed him up in sixth, giving Alpine a double points haul from the heart of the top ten.

Significantly, it has been brought back into play in the fight for P5 in the constructors' championship with Racing Bulls failing to score.

McLaren

McLaren left Las Vegas with both cars on the podium, far exceeding its pre-race prediction.

Lando Norris crossed the line 0.639 seconds behind Verstappen in second, with Oscar Piastri completing the result in third, 1.529 seconds back after starting from P17 on the grid.

Neither driver had the outright pace to trouble Verstappen or Russell through the early lead battle, but McLaren's consistency proved decisive once the Mercedes challenge unravelled.

Both cars benefited directly from Antonelli's late energy deployment problems, moving past the sister Mercedes in the closing laps to turn a solid weekend into a 33-point double finish.

© Red Bull Content Pool

Losers

Ferrari

Ferrari's weekend in Las Vegas descended into farce. Lewis Hamilton was handed a ten-second penalty for leaving the track and gaining a lasting advantage over Norris, before being hit by team-mate Charles Leclerc at Turn 7 on lap 38, a collision that spun Hamilton around and earned Leclerc a further ten-second penalty.

The pair finished seventh and tenth respectively, scoring just seven points between them.

Team principal Frederic Vasseur called the clash completely unacceptable and admitted the tension between his two drivers had become unmanageable over recent rounds, leaving open the question of whether Ferrari will now impose a clearer hierarchy for the final two races of the season.

George Russell

Russell had the pace to win in Las Vegas as he traded the lead with Verstappen across numerous exchanges, using slipstream and energy-deployment strategy to stay in the fight deep into the race.

But the Mercedes driver's challenge ended in the barriers at Turn 5 while attempting to pass team-mate Antonelli, after locking up on dust and debris off the racing line. He eventually crossed the line ninth, salvaging just two points from a weekend that promised so much more.

He was also engaged in another war of words with Max Verstappen - words that likely stung on Saturday night, given their relative positions at the chequered flag.

Racing Bulls

Racing Bulls endured a miserable night in Las Vegas, a day that started with so much promise. Liam Lawson failed to make the starting grid due to a fuel leak, and although he managed to join the race, the damage was done.

Lindblad, meanwhile, looked as though he would secure points for the team before an agonising spin behind the safety car eliminated him from the race.

It proved costly, with Alpine scoring a strong haul of points, leaving the Red Bull junior team looking over its shoulder heading into the final two rounds of the season.

title: Formula E responds after Stellantis pulls plug on Opel and Citroen
excerpt:
Formula E has issued a statement after Stellantis confirmed it will withdraw its Opel and Citroen factory entries from the championship at the end of the 2027 season.

The automotive giant announced the termination of its wider factory motorsport programmes on Monday, a decision that also ends Peugeot's involvement in the World Endurance Championship's Hypercar class.

The move comes as part of chief executive Antonio Filosa's FastLane 2030 strategy, which aims to redirect resources away from works racing and towards customer racing and road-car development.

The Opel GSE Formula E Team only joined the all-electric championship for the current 2027 season, fielding Mitch Evans and Theo Pourchaire under a programme originally pitched as a four-year Gen4 commitment.

That project now faces closure after a single campaign, with no independent team operator in place to take on its powertrain technology.

Citroen's situation differs slightly. Its entry is run by the independently owned MSG Racing outfit, formerly branded Maserati before Stellantis rebranded it last year.

Because MSG Racing holds its own Formula E licence, it is able to pursue external sponsors and a new powertrain supplier to remain on the grid even after Stellantis departs.

Stellantis has also pointed to financial pressure behind the decision, having posted a 311 million euro operating loss in Europe during the third quarter of the year amid price competition from Chinese electric vehicle manufacturers.

Formula E's grid, currently made up of 24 cars across 12 teams, risks shrinking to 20 cars unless replacement manufacturers or buyers emerge before the 2028 season.

Formula E CEO Jeff Dodds said: "We are disappointed by the timing of today’s announcement as Stellantis steps back from factory motorsport amid a period of profound change in the automotive industry.

"We want to reassure our fans, partners and the media that a clear transition will be put in place in accordance with our championship agreements. Opel and Citroën will race in the upcoming 2027 Season, and we thank everyone at Stellantis, Opel and Citroën Racing for their commitment to the championship.

"Looking ahead, Formula E is in its strongest position yet. The arrival of GEN4, an expanded calendar and our global streaming partnership with Disney+ mark the start of our most exciting era."

title: How Red Bull and Max Verstappen outsmarted rivals in blueprint for F1 future
excerpt:
The Las Vegas Grand Prix was defined by something rarely seen in F1: cars running nose to tail not just in the opening laps, but for all 50 laps of the race.

It made for a genuinely unpredictable contest, with position changes rippling through the field from start to finish and keeping the outcome in doubt until the chequered flag.

In many ways, the race felt like a throwback to the start of the 2026 season, before teams had fully refined their energy deployment strategies on the new generation of power units.

But Las Vegas also carried a twist of its own. The slipstream effect on The Strip proved even stronger than at other high-speed venues such as Monza, handing any car following closely a genuine chance of a substantial advantage under braking, and with it, the chance to complete a pass.

The layout of the Las Vegas Strip Circuit, with few genuine braking zones to recharge energy and one long straight running the length of the famous boulevard it is named after, meant each team could tailor a precise deployment strategy to suit its own power unit.

[Article continues below]

Verstappen's late-race request

Notably, in the closing ten laps of the race, Max Verstappen asked his pit wall whether his power unit's energy deployment could be adjusted for the final straight, in search of an advantage over his closest pursuers heading into the last lap.

Red Bull's engineers, however, judged that the existing strategy was already the best available, with the point of maximum energy availability positioned just before the final corner.

In effect, what Verstappen was asking for was already built into the deployment mode chosen for the race.

Simulations and data gathered in practice had given every team a clear picture of which mode to run, based on both starting grid position and the specific characteristics and efficiency of each power unit and chassis.

The proof that this picture was broadly shared across the grid came in the sheer closeness of the field throughout the race, with the top ten cars covered by just three seconds for virtually the entire distance.

It is little surprise, either, that the RB22's performance proved closely matched to that of the Mercedes power unit in terms of raw output.

Mercedes retained a marginal edge in energy recovery, but the Red Bull-Ford unit was able to claw much of that back just past the midpoint of The Strip straight on pure internal combustion power alone.

The Las Vegas Grand Prix laid bare just how closely matched the 2026-specification power units have become, despite each manufacturer taking a different design philosophy to get there.

It is a pattern Formula 1 will hope to see repeated, and even sharpened, across more circuits next season, including those where energy deployment will carry far less weight than it did under the lights on The Strip.

title: Breaking: Formula E faces crisis after astonishing manufacturer group decision
excerpt:
Formula E faces a crisis with two teams being pulled from the championship at the end of 2027 by Stellantis.

Stellantis has confirmed it is winding down its European motorsport programmes, a decision that will see Opel and Citroen depart Formula E at the end of the 2027 season, shortly after the start of the Gen4 era. It will drop Formula E's grid from 24 cars to 20.

The move closes Peugeot's 9X8 Hypercar project in the FIA World Endurance Championship with immediate effect, while it will continue supporting customer racing programmes. This includes Lancia's WRC2 operation and Opel’s electric Corsa and Mokka rally offerings.

Opel's Formula E situation is the most dramatic. The brand has become Formula E's 11th team, with Mitch Evans and Theo Pourchaire signed to drive, having only run pre-season tests at Jarama with its Gen4 car last week. That entry will now run its course through the 2027 season before being wound down.

Citroen's position is slightly less terminal. Its programme is run through the independent Monaco Sports Group organisation rather than as a direct factory operation, in theory leaving the door open for MSG Racing to find a new powertrain partner or commercial backer once Stellantis support ends.

Citroen had only joined the series for Season 12, rebranding Maserati's MSG effort, and had already picked up a win, a pole and a podium. It puts pressure on Formula E to get a Chinese brand involved.

According to Reuters, the cuts form part of chief executive Antonio Filosa's Value Creation Program, which targets six billion euros in group-wide savings by 2028.

Stellantis posted a 311 million euro operating loss in Europe in the third quarter of 2026, with executives pointing to pricing pressure on the continent and intensifying competition from Chinese manufacturers as the driving factors behind the cuts.

© 2026 Getty Images

Why Stellantis has reached this decision

Stellantis has framed the planned withdrawal as part of its wider FastLane 2030 strategy, concentrating corporate resources on customer racing, production vehicles, and cost reductions.

"Stellantis today announced its intention to refocus its motorsport activities and resources on customer racing and high performance vehicle development, while concluding its official motorsport activities at FIA World Championship level," the statement read.

"The decision is consistent with the FaSTLAne 2030 strategic plan, which focuses the company’s efforts and resources on the development of new products, quality and broader market coverage. The five-year plan will include 50 product introductions and updates in Europe, including 25 new products.

"Stellantis intends to retain and redeploy employees impacted by the conclusion of its official FIA World Championship activities, working with them to identify internal opportunities within customer racing, high performance vehicle development and other core activities related to the execution of FaSTLAne 2030."

The company has plans to "retain and redeploy" employees of the Formula E and WEC programmes, although word on how many staff will be impacted as not been published.

Completing the current season rather than withdrawing immediately is understood to be designed to avoid disrupting contracted independent race operators like MSG Racing, giving the teams a transitional runway to secure new commercial partners and powertrain suppliers before the factory support ends.

Notably, the shutdown does not extend to North America, with Dodge's planned factory entry into the NASCAR Cup Series reportedly remaining unaffected.

Whether MSG Racing can secure an alternative powertrain in time to keep Jean-Eric Vergne and Nick Cassidy on the grid beyond the end of the 2027 season remains an open question.

Vasseur went as far as saying "some measures" and "some decisions" must be taken after the incident. The pair also clashed at Monza and in Mexico City.

The Ferrari drivers made contact on Lap 38 in Nevada when Leclerc attempted to pass his team-mate down the inside at Turn 7, sending Hamilton into a spin and capping a miserable weekend for the Maranello-based squad at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit.

It was the second such incident in three races, coming just two weeks after Vasseur held private talks with both drivers to defuse tensions following a first-lap clash in Mexico that cost Ferrari a victory.

Speaking to Sky Sports Italy after the race, Vasseur made clear he held Leclerc responsible for breaching a team instruction not to attempt a move on Hamilton at that stage of the race.

"Clearly, it's unacceptable," he said. "First, [I'll reiterate] the same message from Mexico, because you have to think about the team, about people working in Maranello, about all the stakeholders, the sponsors.

"We passed the message to Charles not to overtake, because in this kind of race, you have to overtake the cars in front of you or you are passed by the others.

"You have to do your race, and Charles clearly made a mistake that has penalised the team a lot; it is completely unacceptable.

"To be honest, I'm more than upset, because the message was clear after Mexico. We’d had a chat all together in Brazil. In the race, we passed the message to think about the team when they were racing together, and the outcome is this one. It's mega frustrating for all of us."

Unlike after Mexico, where Vasseur stressed that Ferrari had failed collectively, the team principal insisted this time that no blame could be laid at the team's door.

Asked whether there was a persistent communication problem between the drivers and the pit wall, including himself, Vasseur rejected the suggestion.

"No, I don't think that's the case. I think the message from the pit wall was very clear," he replied.

"At the end of the day, I'm not the one driving the car, and neither are the track engineers. We gave an order that was crystal clear.

"It's not a question of communication. We'd been very open and very clear after Mexico, and we were the same today."

[Article continues below]

Vassuer: 'If I'd known, our approach would have been different'

Vasseur confirmed that the collision would trigger a fresh internal review in the coming days, and did not rule out punishing one or both drivers.

"We'll discuss this, but we'll certainly have to take some measures and make some decisions," he said. "We don't need to act [immediately]. We must keep calm and then take the necessary steps.

"Of course, it's unacceptable that the work of two thousand people, who put in so much effort, should be ruined in this way. Perhaps it's also time to start thinking about next season."

The comments mark a shift in tone from the Frenchman, who had defended his decision to pair Hamilton with Leclerc as recently as the São Paulo Grand Prix — where crunch talks were held — arguing the pair's fierce competitiveness had helped drive Ferrari to second in the constructors' championship.

But pressed on whether he had expected the rivalry to escalate to this point when he opted to replace Carlos Sainz with the seven-time F1 drivers' champion for 2025, Vasseur gave his clearest indication yet of regret over the pairing.

"Honestly, no. If I'd known, our approach would have been different," he stated. "The pressure is certainly mounting.

"It's much worse now than it was 18 months ago. Lately, the situation between them has become unmanageable. But honestly, ultimately, it's a human misunderstanding between them, not with the team."

title: 2026 F1 Las Vegas Grand Prix Driver Ratings: Who beat their team-mate despite finishing behind?
excerpt:
Check out the driver ratings from RacingNews365 from the 2026 F1 Las Vegas Grand Prix!

23 November 1:00PM

The Las Vegas Grand Prix, and the idiosyncrasies of yo-yo and Peloton-style racing, saw many drivers performing well, and those who did not still had decent weekends — but for moments of madness or mistakes.

One driver's evening in Sin City was so impressive that they outscored their team-mate by a whole mark out of 10, despite finishing behind them.

Check out the full 2026 F1 Las Vegas Grand Prix Driver Ratings from RacingNews365 below!

Top five

Max Verstappen - 10

Back-to-back 10/10s for Verstappen and three in the last five rounds. No surprise, really. Inherited pole, but look at what he did with it. Outfoxed the opposition with Red Bull also one step ahead of their rivals, and — despite the frenetic, breathless yo-yo/peloton-style race — you always got the sense he would prevail. Won't go into the various things he said about George Russell afterwards; don't want to take the shine off.

Oscar Piastri - 9

Yet again outmatched by Lando Norris in qualifying, and there was little Piastri could have done about his 10-place grid penalty. However, having started from P17, he carved through the field where he met his McLaren team-mate, who had begun dropping like a stone. From there, they worked brilliantly together to slice through the pack ahead, getting in position to capitalise on a dreadful couple of laps from the Mercedes drivers. A hard-earned and overdue podium for the Australian. Coming from so far back and saving the race of Norris, who finished ahead of him in second, aids his high score.

Pierre Gasly - 8.5

Gasly is becoming somewhat of a Las Vegas Strip Circuit specialist, and this weekend was no exception. Alpine enjoyed a little renaissance in Sin City, with both drivers reaching Q3 for the first time since the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. Come the race, the Frenchman was superb, keeping in the hunt with the lead pack, taking the chequered flag in fifth, fewer than three seconds behind winner Verstappen.

Carlos Sainz - 8.5

Starting P20, very few would have bet on Sainz finishing eighth, given the far-reaching issues with this year's Williams. But the Spaniard put together a terrific first lap to latch onto the fight for points and, from there, was calm and calculated — as all the drivers had to be, given the demands of the race — to make the most of mistakes and moments of madness from those ahead. Valuable points in a dismal campaign for his team.

Franco Colapinto - 8

Just when Colapinto really needed a result, he delivered. A shade off what Gasly was able to do in the sister car, but that isn't to be wholly unexpected. F1 is plagued by recency bias, and despite a decent season, the 23-year-old finds himself under pressure of late. After all, you're only as good as your last race. With speculation of Ollie Bearman (who also scored an 8/10) sniffing around his seat and rumours of Flavio Briatore's patience wearing thin, this performance might just save his F1 career.

Bottom five

Fernando Alonso - 4.5

It might be a smidgen harsh to give Alonso a whole mark less than Lance Stroll, given the two-time F1 drivers' champion again — as always — had the upper hand in the intra-Aston Martin battle. But you come to expect more from the Spaniard, and his mysterious decision to retire at quite literally the final corner of the race, citing a broken power unit, has been publicly questioned by Honda. It's a curious case at the end of a long, hard season, with a particularly bleak winter ahead. That said, he was subpar compared to his usual high standards.

Arvid Lindblad - 4

It was going so well! And then... and then it wasn't. This will be a painful one for Lindblad to take, and he said as much after the race. But he knows, and I know (and you know), that you simply cannot inexplicably drop your car when behind the safety car, no matter how difficult the conditions are, or whether you've just had a bad downshift. The rest of the weekend, the Racing Bulls driver was sensational and was outperforming Liam Lawson in the sister car. Maybe that makes what was, quite fittingly, a rookie error all the more egregious.

Sergio Perez - 4

Was quicker than Valtteri Bottas in the other Cadillac. But his team-mate didn't needlessly punt a driver, in just their second F1 race, off the circuit, causing his own retirement from the grand prix in the process. Not Perez's finest moment. Thoughts are with Rafael Camara, but no need to linger on it.

George Russell - 4

Could have won. Didn't win. Careless error two laps from home robbed him of the opportunity and left his fight for second in the drivers' championship in tatters. A late mistake is something we've seen before from Russell. Yes, there was debris in the braking zone, but he almost collected Kimi Antonelli in the process. Got better at racing Verstappen as the evening progressed, but never quite had the measure of the Red Bull driver. Two points isn't enough when it should have been at the very least a podium.

Charles Leclerc - 4

There is so much that could, should and will be said about the current state of affairs at Ferrari, and Leclerc's part in what is quite quickly escalating into a full-blown crisis. However, in just a few short sentences: The Monegasque driver has to have a really honest conversation with himself about how he races Lewis Hamilton and what he wants to be remembered for. A nine-time grand prix winner, he has the talent to win titles. But he never will if he doesn't rein it in and stop alienating those around him.

title: Max Verstappen 'from a different planet' as shocked Red Bull left asking questions
excerpt:
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has voiced his amazement over Max Verstappen's abilities following his victory at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The four-time champion secured his 75th career victory in a highly dramatic race that saw 34 different overtakes for the lead.

Verstappen was forced to battle several drivers for the lead throughout the 50 laps, including team-mate Isack Hadjar, the Mercedes duo of George Russell and Kimi Antonelli, and McLaren's Lando Norris.

The heightened slipstream effect at the grand prix saw Verstappen being overtaken into Turn 14 before he got back past into the final corner or the first turn.

When it was raised to Mekies that perhaps Verstappen's wheel-to-wheel combat is an area he doesn't get enough credit for, Mekies told media including RacingNews365: "Absolutely, you are spot on there.

"We are coming from Brazil, and what he did in Brazil felt normal to everyone where it was completely mind-blowing.

"You come here, and he was asking us questions about the last lap at 10 laps to go.

"Look at the race today, look at the race in Brazil. Look at the way he positioned his car relative to the others."

Verstappen leaving Red Bull stunned

Verstappen's race in Brazil saw him climb from 21st on the starting grid to second place at the chequered flag.

After his calculated route to victory on Saturday night in Las Vegas, Mekies stated Verstappen is still finding ways to surprise the Red Bull team.

"He is always at the perfect pace, at the perfect moment. Yes, it's surprising us every day.

"Every race on the pit wall, we look at each other and we say, 'What was that?'

"That's really what we do. I don't know if you want to call it underrated because I don't think he is underrated.

"He's from a different planet."

title: George Russell warned after Max Verstappen spat: 'He will beat the **** out of you'
excerpt:
Former Haas F1 team principal Guenther Steiner has suggested George Russell should back down from aggravating Max Verstappen going forward.

The duo got into a spat during the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend after an on-track incident during final practice, after which Russell stated that "someone has to stand up" to Verstappen.

Two years ago, the pair launched into a war of words at the end of the campaign and traded blows through the media, a feud that was reignited last weekend.

Max Verstappen pulled no punches after his victory on Sunday in Las Vegas, stating Russell is "so far below my level" and that the Mercedes driver's poor race result was "karma".

Steiner suggested Russell should change his approach, insisting he is fighting a losing battle against Verstappen.

"I haven't got a problem with that because in the end, if they don't like each other, what do I care?" Steiner told the Red Flags podcast.

"This is going on for a long time between them, and obviously George coming out to say, 'this guy behaves very arrogantly' and 'somebody needs to stand up to him', yeah, good luck with that one, buddy.

"You see how that worked out. I respect George as a race car driver, but in the end, Max, mentally is just superior.

"How he manages mental things, he is so superior to you. Do not poke the bear, in my opinion.

"There is no need for it because you don't do yourself any favours. Get over it, try to win races instead of picking a battle with the best driver out there, with the strongest mental guy out there.

"Because guess what? You're going to lose. I don't understand that George has nobody around him telling him, 'George, pick on somebody else'.

"Max will beat the shit out of you anyway, driving-wise and in a fight of words.”

[Article continues below]

Steiner encourages intervention amid Russell 'weak position'

Russell was in contention for the race victory in Las Vegas before a late-race mistake saw him lock up and lightly hit the barrier.

It marked another disappointing moment for him during a challenging season in which he was forced to witness his team-mate Kimi Antonelli cruise to championship success.

Steiner highlighted that Russell needs a voice in his ear to guide him away from such battles.

"At a certain stage in your life, you need to know that if you can't beat them, join them. There is no messenger," he said.

"And if you try to do the thing you can't message, and you know you will just be losing out, why do you do it?

"There is nobody out as talented and as mentally strong as Max. So whoever does it will be a loser.

"Why is George trying to pick that one? What does he want to prove? You're in a very weak position.

"You just lost the world championship, and now you want to bust the balls of one of the best of the best drivers in the world championship.

"Come on, George, sit back. But that's what I mean, nobody is sitting down with him and saying, 'George, sometimes less is more. Just say nothing. Do your own job. Get back to winning races and when you have got something to say because you beat the guy, pick your battle.'

"If you cannot beat them, join them. At the moment, just shut up and get on with it. That's what I would be doing.

"Max is enjoying it."

title: What action should Ferrari take after the latest clash between Hamilton and Leclerc?
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc was handed a 10-second penalty after a clash with team-mate Lewis Hamilton at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, the latest flashpoint in a season of simmering tension between the two Ferrari drivers.

Leclerc attempted an inside move on Hamilton into Turn 7, ran wide across the kerb and clipped the Briton's car, spinning him and costing both drivers positions.

FIA stewards found Leclerc wholly to blame, ruling he had approached from too far back to have earned the corner. Hamilton recovered to finish seventh, with Leclerc down in tenth.

Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur condemned the incident as completely unacceptable over the radio and called an immediate meeting with Leclerc before the Monegasque faced the media.

It is not the first time the pair have come to blows this season. At the Mexico City Grand Prix, a first-lap fight at Turn 4 sent both cars off track, earning Leclerc a five-second penalty and costing Ferrari a likely one-two behind Max Verstappen.

Hamilton later accused his team-mate of a do-or-die mentality, triggering crisis talks overseen by Vasseur in São Paulo. Earlier flashpoints in China, the Netherlands and Italy also saw aggressive wheel-to-wheel racing and radio complaints between the two.
